title: Before the Rails
summary: Long ago, moving heavy things over land was slow, muddy, tiring work for people and animals. Clever builders in ancient Greece cut grooves into a stone road to drag ships across land, and German miners pushed carts along wooden planks. These were the first baby steps toward the railway!

sections.heading: A World at Walking Speed
paragraphs: Close your eyes and imagine you live five hundred years ago. You want to visit a town 50 kilometres away. There is no train, no bus, no car and no bicycle. You can walk, which takes all day and leaves your feet aching. If your family is rich, you might ride a horse. Either way, the fastest you can possibly travel over land is the speed of a galloping horse, and no horse can gallop for long. For almost all of human history, that was simply how the world worked.

Moving people was hard. Moving heavy things was much harder. For thousands of years, goods went from place to place in three main ways: on the backs of people, on the backs of animals, or in carts and wagons pulled by animals. Where there was a river or a coast, a fourth way was available, and it was often the best one: put the load in a boat and let the water carry the weight.

In Britain, a common way to move goods across hilly country was the packhorse train. A line of sturdy ponies, often 12 to 20 of them and sometimes as many as 40, walked nose to tail along narrow tracks. Each pony carried two baskets or bags called panniers, slung on either side of its back, holding about 110 kilograms in total. The lead pony often wore a bell so that anyone coming the other way would hear the train approaching and get out of the way. A good packhorse train covered about 40 kilometres a day.

Some packhorse routes were astonishingly busy. Records from northern England describe 200 to 300 loaded horses a day crossing one river ford in the 1630s, and about a thousand packhorses a day passing through the town of Clitheroe before 1750. You can still walk over old packhorse bridges in the English countryside today. They are narrow stone arches with low walls, just wide enough for a pony with bulging panniers, because nobody expected a wagon to use them.

Why not just use wagons? Because the roads were terrible. Most roads were not built at all; they were simply paths that people and animals had walked along for centuries. In dry summer weather they were bumpy and dusty. In wet weather they turned into deep, sticky mud. Heavy wheels sank in, and every passing wagon churned the mud deeper. Deep grooves called ruts formed where the wheels always ran, and in winter some roads became completely impossible for wheeled vehicles. A wagon stuck axle-deep in mud could take a whole team of horses and several men to haul out.

So whenever they could, people used water. A single boat floating on a river could carry many tons, and the water did the hard work of holding up the weight. That is why so many old towns grew up beside rivers and harbours. But rivers only go where rivers go. If your load was somewhere inland, far from water, you were stuck with the slow, muddy, expensive road.

sections.heading: The Problem of Heavy Things
paragraphs: Some loads are light but valuable, like spices, silk, letters or gold coins. It is worth paying a lot to move a small bag of pepper, because the pepper sells for a high price. Other loads are heavy but cheap: coal, stone, bricks, timber, grain, iron ore and lime for farmers' fields. A ton of coal was not worth very much at the mine. If it cost more to haul it a few kilometres than the coal itself was worth, then nobody would bother.

Think about what that meant for a coal mine. Coal could keep homes warm and fuel forges and furnaces, but it is extremely heavy. A family might burn several tons in a winter. A packhorse carrying about 110 kilograms would need around nine trips just to move one ton. Even a horse pulling a cart on a dry road could only manage a load of perhaps a ton or so, and on a wet, rutted road far less. Each trip needed the horse, its food, a driver, and time. All of that cost money, and the price of coal rose quickly the farther it travelled from the pit.

This was true of building stone, too. Great cathedrals and castles were often built close to quarries, or close to rivers that could float the stone to the building site. Farmers who wanted to sell grain in a distant city faced the same problem: the journey ate up the profit. In a very real way, the speed and cost of moving heavy things decided where towns grew, which industries could exist, and how big a business could become.

Here is the key point, which you will meet again and again in this story. The problem was not really the weight itself. The problem was the friction and the mud. A wheel that sinks into soft ground is always trying to climb out of a little hole that it has made in front of itself. A wheel bumping over stones wastes energy with every jolt. Take away the mud and the bumps, and the very same horse can suddenly pull a far heavier load. People had noticed this for thousands of years. The question was how to build a surface that stayed hard, smooth and in the right place.

sections.heading: The Diolkos: Dragging Ships Across Greece
paragraphs: One of the earliest and most impressive answers comes from ancient Greece. Look at a map of Greece and you will see a big chunk of land in the south, the Peloponnese, joined to the mainland by a narrow neck of land called the Isthmus of Corinth. At its narrowest point the isthmus is only about 6 kilometres wide. On one side is the Gulf of Corinth, leading west toward Italy. On the other side is the Saronic Gulf, leading east toward Athens and the Aegean Sea.

For a sailor, going all the way around the Peloponnese by sea meant a voyage of hundreds of kilometres, including the rocky and stormy capes at the southern tip, which had a fearsome reputation for wrecking ships. Wouldn't it be wonderful if you could simply take your ship, or at least its cargo, straight across the narrow neck of land?

Around 600 BCE, the people of Corinth did exactly that. They built the Diolkos, a name that roughly means 'haul-across'. It was a paved road made of hard limestone blocks that ran from one sea to the other, about 6 to 8.5 kilometres long depending on how its bends are measured. Archaeologists think it was built in the late 7th or early 6th century BCE, around the time when a ruler named Periander governed Corinth. The road was between about 3.4 and 6 metres wide.

The clever part was cut into the stone itself. Along long stretches of the Diolkos run two parallel grooves, about 1.6 metres apart. The wheels of a heavy wooden vehicle fitted into these grooves, which kept the vehicle on course, rather like a toy train running in the slots of a wooden track. The haulers did not have to steer. They just had to pull. Some researchers think parts of the grooves were deliberately cut, while others think some sections were simply worn down by centuries of wheels. Either way, the result was a guided path for heavy loads.

How was a ship moved? Historians cannot be completely sure, because no ancient writer left a detailed instruction manual. The most likely idea is that a ship, or its cargo, was lifted onto a wheeled cart or cradle at one end and then hauled across by teams of men, and perhaps by animals, using ropes. Machines called capstans, a kind of winch turned by people pushing on bars, may also have helped. The route had to climb over a ridge about 79 metres high, but its slope was gentle, averaging only about 1.4 percent, meaning it rose about 1.4 metres for every 100 metres travelled. The steepest parts were around 6 percent.

Most of the time the Diolkos probably carried cargo and smaller boats. But ancient writers describe warships being dragged across too. The Athenian historian Thucydides wrote that the Spartans prepared to haul ships across the isthmus in 428 BCE, and again in 411 BCE. Much later, in 220 BCE, a commander named Demetrius of Pharos is said to have taken about 50 vessels across. A modern engineering study estimated that a trireme, a long warship about 35 metres long with three banks of oars, might have weighed about 25 tonnes and needed well over a hundred people pulling hard to cross. It could be done, but it was a struggle.

The Diolkos stayed in use for a very long time, from around 600 BCE until at least the middle of the 1st century CE, more than 600 years. The ancient playwright Aristophanes even made a joke about something moving 'as fast as a Corinthian', a sign that the trackway was famous across Greece. The Roman emperor Nero later tried to dig a proper canal across the isthmus in 67 CE, but the project was abandoned.

The ship canal finally arrived in modern times: the Corinth Canal opened in 1893, running right beside the remains of the old trackway. Greek archaeologist Nikolaos Verdelis excavated the Diolkos between 1956 and 1962 and uncovered a nearly continuous stretch about 800 metres long. Sadly, the wash from passing ships has since eroded parts of it, and repair work to protect the site was carried out as recently as 2024.

Was the Diolkos a railway? Not in the modern sense. It had no rails of metal or wood, no engines, and it was a single special route rather than a network. But it shared the most important idea of all railways: a hard, fixed, guided path that makes it much easier to move a heavy load and keeps it going where you want it to go. It is one of the earliest known 'guided ways' in history.

sections.heading: Ruts, Grooves and the Science of a Smooth Path
paragraphs: The Diolkos was special, but grooves in the ground were not unusual in the ancient world. Wherever heavy carts travelled the same route year after year, their wheels wore tracks into the road. Walk down a street in the Roman town of Pompeii, buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, and you can still see deep ruts worn into the big paving stones by countless cart wheels. Once ruts like these exist, they act a little like rails: a cart drops into them and tends to follow them.

On the Mediterranean island of Malta there are even stranger tracks. Pairs of parallel grooves are cut into bare rock across the countryside, sometimes crossing and branching so much that one site has been nicknamed 'Clapham Junction', after a famously busy railway junction in London. Nobody is completely sure who made them, when, or exactly how. Archaeologists still argue about whether they were worn by carts, sledges or something else, and estimates of their age vary widely. They are a good reminder that history is full of real puzzles that have not been solved yet.

Paved trackways were also built in Roman Egypt, and Roman engineers were famous for their well-built roads. A good Roman road had layers of stone and gravel underneath and a hard, cambered surface on top, so rainwater ran off instead of turning it to mud. That was the same idea from another direction: if you cannot build a groove, at least build a surface that stays hard and dry.

Why does a hard, smooth, fixed path help so much? Let's do a quick experiment in your head. Push a toy car across a thick, fluffy carpet. It slows down and stops almost at once. Now push it across a smooth wooden floor. It rolls a long way. The car and your push are exactly the same. What changed is the surface. On the carpet, the wheels squash down into the fibres and have to keep climbing over them. On the hard floor there is almost nothing in the way.

Scientists call this rolling resistance. Whenever a wheel rolls, both the wheel and the surface underneath it squash a tiny bit. The softer they are, the more they squash, and the more energy is wasted. Mud is the worst of all: a heavy wheel sinks in and is always pushing a little wall of mud in front of it. Stones and potholes are bad too, because every bump lifts the load slightly and then drops it, wasting effort and shaking the cart to pieces.

A smooth, hard track solves both problems at once. The wheels barely sink in, and there are no bumps to climb. A guided track, with grooves or raised edges, adds a third bonus: the vehicle cannot wander off sideways, so it can be pulled without anyone steering, and it always runs on the strong part of the track instead of the soft verge. Keep those three ideas in mind, hard, smooth and guided, because they are the secret recipe of every railway that came afterwards, right up to today's high-speed trains.

sections.heading: Dogs in the Mines: Agricola's Wooden Tracks
paragraphs: Now let's jump forward about two thousand years, to the busy mining towns of central Europe in the 1500s. In the mountains along the border of what are now Germany and the Czech Republic, miners dug deep tunnels to reach silver, copper, tin and lead. Silver from these mines was so important that a coin minted in the town of Joachimsthal (today Jáchymov in the Czech Republic) was called the Joachimsthaler, later shortened to 'thaler'. That name travelled around the world and eventually turned into the word 'dollar'.

Underground, miners had a big problem: how to move broken rock and ore along narrow, dark, uneven tunnels. Their solution was a small wooden wagon on four wheels, pushed by a person. To stop it from getting stuck or veering into the tunnel walls, they laid two wooden planks along the floor with a narrow gap between them. A peg, or guide pin, sticking down from the bottom of the wagon slid along in the gap, keeping the wagon on course. The wheels themselves were plain, with no rims to grip the planks. The guide pin did all the steering.

German miners called these wagons 'Hunde', meaning 'dogs'. One common explanation is that the rumbling, squeaking noise they made as they rattled along the planks sounded like a dog barking or growling. Whether or not that is the true reason, the nickname stuck, and mine wagons in parts of Europe were called 'dogs' for centuries.

We know about these carts mainly thanks to one remarkable man. Georg Bauer was born in 1494 in Saxony, in eastern Germany. Like many scholars of his time, he wrote in Latin and used a Latin version of his name: Georgius Agricola. Bauer means 'farmer' in German, and agricola means 'farmer' in Latin. He trained as a doctor and worked as a town physician, first in Joachimsthal and later in the mining city of Chemnitz. But he was fascinated by the mines around him. He spent years watching miners at work, asking questions and studying their tools and machines.

The result was a huge book called De re metallica, Latin for 'On the Nature of Metals'. It covered everything about mining and metal-making at the time: how to find ore, how to dig and survey tunnels, how to pump water out of mines, how to lift ore to the surface, how to wash, roast and smelt it, and much more. It was divided into twelve parts called books and filled with about 292 detailed woodcut pictures. Agricola died in 1555, and the book was finally published in Basel, Switzerland, in 1556, a year after his death. Making all those woodcuts had taken a long time.

Among its pictures is a famous image of a Hund: a small, boxy wooden wagon on planks, with the pin underneath that kept it on track. It is one of the earliest clear drawings of a wagon running on a prepared track. The book also shows enormous wooden machines driven by water wheels and by horses walking in circles, used to pump water and to lift loads out of deep shafts. These were some of the most advanced machines in the world at that time.

De re metallica was so useful that it stayed the most important book about mining in Europe for about 180 years. It was translated into German in 1557, Italian in 1563 and Spanish in 1569. The first English translation did not appear until 1912, and it was made by a husband-and-wife team, the mining engineer Herbert Hoover and the geologist Lou Henry Hoover. Herbert Hoover later became the 31st President of the United States.

sections.heading: Tracks Begin to Spread
paragraphs: The mines of central Europe were not the only places experimenting with tracks. High above the Austrian city of Salzburg stands Hohensalzburg Fortress, one of the largest medieval castles in Europe. To get supplies up the steep hill, its builders made a little goods line called the Reisszug. It was described in writing in 1515 by Matthäus Lang, a churchman who later became archbishop and ruler of Salzburg, though it may be even older. It used wooden rails, and its wagon was hauled up the slope by a rope made of hemp. The power came from people or animals turning a treadwheel, a large wheel that you walk inside, like a giant hamster wheel.

Amazingly, the Reisszug still exists. It is about 190 metres long and still carries goods up to the fortress, although today it has steel rails, a steel cable and an electric motor instead of wooden rails, hemp and treadwheel power. Human or animal power was used until 1910. Because of its long history, some people describe it as perhaps the oldest railway still operating in the world.

Mining know-how travelled with miners. In the 1560s, German miners were invited to work copper and lead mines in the Lake District, in north-west England, and they brought their skills with them, very likely including wheeled tubs on wooden tracks. Tracked transport at Caldbeck in Cumbria, perhaps from the 1560s, is thought to be among the earliest in Britain.

Notice something important about all these early tracks. They were short, they were mostly underground or on private land, and they were pushed by people or pulled by ropes or animals. Nobody yet imagined a track running for kilometres across open fields. And nobody imagined an engine. Engines powerful enough to move themselves were still more than two centuries in the future. But the basic idea, wheels guided along a smooth prepared path, was spreading, and in Britain it was about to meet the perfect customer: coal.

sections.heading: The Big Idea That Runs Through This Whole Story
paragraphs: Let's pause and look at what we have learned, because it is the key to everything that follows in all twenty parts of this story.

On a rough road, a horse struggles to pull even a modest load, because so much of its effort is wasted fighting mud, bumps and friction. Put that same horse on a hard, smooth, guided track, and the wasted effort drops dramatically. On a good track, one horse can pull many times more weight than it could on a dirt road. You will see real numbers for this in the next part, when horses begin hauling coal wagons on wooden rails in England.

That one simple fact changed the economics of heavy goods. If one horse can do the work of many, then coal, stone and iron become cheaper to move. Cheaper coal means warmer homes and more fuel for furnaces and workshops. More furnaces mean more iron. More iron means better tools and machines. Step by step, the humble track helped push forward the huge changes that historians call the Industrial Revolution.

And here is the part that will matter most later on. A smooth track does not only help horses. It helps anything that pulls. When inventors finally built engines that could move by themselves, those engines were heavy and not very powerful at first. On a muddy road they would have sunk and stalled. On a track, they could pull. The railway engine and the rail were made for each other. Without the track, the steam locomotive might never have succeeded at all.

So the railway was not invented in one flash by one genius. It grew slowly, over many centuries, from ruts in roads, grooves in stone, planks in mine tunnels and ropes on castle hills. Each idea was small. Put together, they would one day carry billions of people around the world.

Our next stop is England in the early 1600s. Coal was becoming more and more valuable as forests were cut down and wood grew scarce. In the coalfields of the English Midlands and the north-east, mine owners were looking for a better way to get their heavy black fuel from the pit to the river. And for the first time, miners were about to lay wooden rails above ground, out in the open air, stretching across the fields.

deepDive: What counts as the 'first railway'? It depends entirely on your definition, and historians use several. If a railway is any prepared path that guides wheels, then the Diolkos of Corinth, built around 600 BCE, is a strong candidate, along with grooved roads in other parts of the ancient world. If it must have rails, separate strips that the wheels run on, then the wooden planks of central European mines in the 1500s, shown in Agricola's De re metallica (1556), qualify, as does the rope-hauled Reisszug in Salzburg, first described in 1515. If it must run overland and carry goods for trade, the English wagonways of the early 1600s come next. If it must use engines, we have to wait until 1804. None of these answers is wrong; they simply answer different questions. The Diolkos itself is surrounded by debate. Its length is given as anything from about 6 to 8.5 kilometres because parts of the route have been lost and scholars disagree about its bends. The grooves, roughly 1.6 metres apart, look like a deliberate guide on some stretches, but some researchers argue the western grooves are simply wear from centuries of wheels. Nobody knows exactly how ships were mounted on the vehicles, how often warships really crossed, or whether animals helped. Engineering estimates for hauling a 25-tonne trireme range from over a hundred people to a smaller team using capstans, and the experts disagree. The excavator, Nikolaos Verdelis, died before he could fully publish his 1956–1962 findings, which is one reason these questions remain open. The physics, however, is not in doubt. A wheel's rolling resistance depends heavily on how much the wheel and surface deform. Soft ground deforms a lot, so a horse on mud spends most of its effort on squashing and climbing. Stone, wood and later iron deform very little. Add a guide that prevents sideways drift, and a vehicle can carry far more weight for the same pulling force. That principle, minimal deformation plus guidance, is the thread that connects ancient grooves to modern steel rails.
funFact: The first English translation of Agricola's great mining book De re metallica was published in 1912 by Herbert Hoover and his wife Lou Henry Hoover, years before he became President of the United States.
